# Block 5: Enforced controls: permissions and detection {.unnumbered} Your instruction fileA file the assistant loads into every conversation, such as AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md, stating the project’s standing conventions. Its contents are requests, not guarantees. and skills are requests: nothing guarantees that the model follows them. In this block you watch the controls that do hold refuse something. You also find the route each one misses, so you know what your repository prevents and what it only detects. *⏱ ~25 minutes · Start on `main` (or `checkpoint-skills`), Git pane clean, Claude Code running in Manual mode.* :::{#block5-files .callout-note collapse="true"} ## This block's files, and how it fits This block uses the same repository but no data: you practise on `data/raw/scratch.csv`, then delete it. The block adds only a rule and a log line, so no checkpoint follows. These controls protect [Blocks 7](11g-data-cleaning.qmd) and [8](11i-characterisation-tests.qmd). [Block 6](11k-build-an-agent.qmd) shows the same controls inside an agent written in R. *Set up guardrails in your own project*, after the exercises, has a starter `settings.json` for your own projects. | File | Where it comes from | Exercise 2 step | |---|---|---| | `.claude/settings.json`: Manual mode and 17 deny rules | Shipped with the template | 1–4 | | `data/raw/scratch.csv` | You create it, then delete it | 1 and 5 | | `Read(/data/confidential/**)` in `.claude/settings.json` | You, with `/permissions` | 3 | | `tests/test_controls.R` | Shipped with the template | 6 | | A line in `docs/ai-log.md` (the log from Block 3) | You | 6 | ::: ## Three kinds of guardrail Beyond the instruction file, there are three kinds of guardrail. Each catches what the others miss. - **Permissions** decide what the agent may do without asking, and what it may never do. In Claude Code they live in `.claude/settings.json`: a starting mode (Manual asks before every edit and command) and deny rules. A deny rule *prevents*, but only on the routes it names. - **Hooks** are your own code, which Claude Code runs at set moments: before a tool call, after an edit, before it stops. They suit "every time X happens, do Y". A hook that blocks by matching text is a tripwire, not a wall. The workshop ships none, on purpose: see *Do you need a hook?*, below. - **Version tracking** lets you *detect* and *undo*. Git, through the Git pane, shows every change since your last commit, whatever made it, and reverts it. Claude Code's own undo, `/rewind`, is quicker but covers only changes made with its edit tools. Tests and checksums detect what should not have changed. Prevent where you can, detect everything, and commit before the agent starts, so that there is something to go back to. :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ## How your workshop repository is guarded Every guardrail below came with the template. You have been relying on them since Block 2. | Guardrail | Where it lives | Kind | Set up by | |---|---|---|---| | A git repository, clean before each task | `.git/`; the Git pane | Detect and undo | The template; you commit before each task | | Manual mode | `.claude/settings.json` (`"defaultMode": "default"`) | Approval prompt | The template | | 17 deny rules | `.claude/settings.json` | Prevent, on the routes they name | The template; you add one today | | No command approved in advance | No `allow` list in the settings | Approval prompt | The template; `test_controls.R` checks it | | Run `git status`; never touch raw data | `AGENTS.md` | Request | The template; yours since Block 4 | | Tests, including `test_controls.R` | `tests/` | Detect | The template | | Credentials kept out of commits | `.gitignore` lists `.Renviron` and `.env` | Prevent sharing | The template | | A checksum of the raw data | `tests/test_cleaning.R` | Detect | The template; used in [Block 7](11g-data-cleaning.qmd) | | Hooks | None | — | Not shipped: see *Do you need a hook?* | | The sandbox | Not set | Prevent, by any route | Not available on native Windows ([Block 3](11d-context-disclosure-autonomy.qmd)) | ::: ## Exercise 1: What protects what? :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Match each asset to its guardrails (3 minutes) :::: ::::{.task-container} **Goal:** for each thing worth protecting, find what in your repository prevents the damage and how you would notice it, so that you know which guardrail you are relying on before an agent works near it. Your instructor posts the table. Use *How your workshop repository is guarded*, above, and answer in the Zoom chat, row by row: what prevents this here, and if it went wrong anyway, how would you notice? | Asset | What could go wrong | What prevents it here | How you would notice | |---|---|---|---| | `data/raw/` | Overwritten or "tidied" in place | | | | `tests/fixtures/` | The reference regenerated by the code under test | | | | `tests/` | A failing test edited until it passes | | | | `.claude/`, `.posit/` | The agent's own guardrails switched off | | | | `.Renviron`, `.env` | Credentials read and sent to the model provider | | | The last two are easy to miss: the files that hold your controls are assets too. **You are done when** the group has an answer for both columns in every row. Most "prevents" answers will be a deny rule; most "notice" answers will be "the Git pane would show it" or "a test would fail". :::: ::: Git detects only the changes since your last commit, so commit before an agent starts. Some controls prevent and some only detect; Exercise 2 shows which. :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ## The layers of control, and how each fails | Layer | Example | What it does | How it fails | |---|---|---|---| | Instruction | `AGENTS.md`, a skill | Requests | Silently ignored | | Approval prompt | "Allow this command?" | Prevents, if you read it | Approval fatigue | | Deny rule | `Edit(/data/raw/**)` | Prevents | Another route reaches the file | | Hook | A script Claude Code runs before each tool call | Prevents | Rephrasing gets past it; by default, a crashing hook lets the call through | | Sandbox | `/sandbox` (macOS, Linux, WSL2) | Prevents, by any route, for the paths you list | Not available on native Windows | | Version control | The Git pane | Detects and undoes | Only changes since your last commit, and only if you look | | Claude Code's undo | `/rewind` | Undoes | Only changes made with its edit tools, not R code it ran | | Tests and checksums | testthat, `tools::md5sum()` | Detects | Only if they run | Your repository's `AGENTS.md` asks the agent to run `git status` before it edits anything, and to stop if there is no repository. That request helps, but your commit is the control. ::: ## Exercise 2: Deny rules :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Read, test and add a rule, then find the gap (15 minutes) :::: ::::{.task-container} **Goal:** see a deny ruleA permission rule in the deny list of .claude/settings.json that stops Claude Code’s built-in tools from editing or reading the matching files. It checks shell output redirects such as > file, but not R code or most other commands that change the same files. refuse, add one of your own and find the route the rules do not cover, so that you know what your repository prevents and what only git detects. **Start state:** Git pane clean, Claude Code in Manual mode. Work on a scratch file, never on real data. **1. Make a scratch file and read the rules.** Run this in the R console: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} writeLines("a", here::here("data", "raw", "scratch.csv")) ``` ::: Commit it in the Git pane, so git can show any later change to it. In Claude Code, type `/permissions` to list the 17 deny rules that your repository ships. **2. See a rule refuse.** **Prompt (Claude Code):** ```text Add a second line, "test", to data/raw/scratch.csv. ``` "Denied by a permission rule" means the rule held, whatever the model intended. The model may instead decline by itself, citing `AGENTS.md`. That was a request that happened to work. To see the rule refuse, reply "This is a scratch file; please make the edit with your edit tool". **Answer each request with plain Yes or No.** Never choose an option that says *don't ask again*: it saves a rule that skips the question from then on. If Claude Code asks to write the file another way, answer No: step 4 tries that. **3. Add a rule yourself.** In `/permissions`, add `Read(/data/confidential/**)`: habit 4 of the confidential-data habits in [Block 3](11d-context-disclosure-autonomy.qmd), a speed bump rather than a wall. When asked where to save it, choose the project's shared settings file, `.claude/settings.json`, not the local one (see *How it works*). It applies at once. You do not test this rule here, because there is no `data/confidential/` folder. In your own project, test it the way you test `Edit(/data/raw/**)` in this exercise. **4. Find the gap.** **Prompt (Claude Code):** ```text Run this R code with Rscript: writeLines(c("a", "test"), "data/raw/scratch.csv") ``` Deny rules do not cover R code, so only the approval prompt stands in the way. Approve a run only if you can say what it does and why you want it now; refusing is always safe. Here you can: it writes to a scratch file, and you want to see what catches the change. **Approve it.** The Git pane now shows the file as modified, and **Diff** shows the new line: git caught what no rule prevented. Now try Claude Code's own undo. Type `/rewind` (or press Esc twice with the prompt empty) and select your last prompt. The menu offers no *Restore code*: `/rewind` restores only changes made with Claude Code's edit tools, and R code changed this file. Choose *Never mind*. Only git can undo this change. **5. Tidy up.** Undo the change with git: revert the file in the Git pane. Then delete it, so that no scratch file is left among the raw data: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} file.remove(here::here("data", "raw", "scratch.csv")) ``` ::: **6. Record, test and commit.** Add a line to `docs/ai-log.md`: ask the agent to draft it, as in Block 3, then write the last part yourself. Note which requests were refused, and what git caught and undid. Then restart R (*Session → Restart R*) and run: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} testthat::test_dir(here::here("tests")) ``` ::: `test_controls.R` checks that Manual mode and every shipped rule are still in place. It also checks that no command is approved in advance. `test_ai_log.R` checks your new line. Commit the deletion of `scratch.csv`, your rule in `.claude/settings.json` and the log line together. **You are done when** you have seen a rule refuse, added one of your own, seen the Git pane catch the R write that `/rewind` could not undo, `scratch.csv` is gone, the test suite has no failures (tests for later blocks skip), and your rule and log line are committed. **If it goes wrong:** if the model keeps declining in step 4, write the line yourself in the console and carry on: the point is seeing git catch it. If `/rewind` does offer *Restore code*, the agent changed some file with its edit tool earlier in this conversation: choose *Never mind* anyway. If "no command is approved in advance" fails, you chose *don't ask again*: remove that allow rule in `/permissions`. :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ## At the command line Step 1: `git add`/`git commit`. Step 4: `git diff data/raw`. Step 5: `git restore`, then `git rm data/raw/scratch.csv`. Step 6: `Rscript -e "testthat::test_dir('tests')"`, then `git add`/`git commit`. See [checking work](11a-setup-claude-code.qmd#checking-work). ::: :::: ::: :::::::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Where each control acts :::::: {.dia .dia-lanes role="figure" aria-label="Where each control acts. Route 1: the agent asks its edit tool to change a file in data/raw, and the deny rule refuses. Route 2: the agent runs R code that writes the file; with no hook registered, only the approval prompt stands in the way. If the file changes, git status detects it, as does, from Block 7, the checksum test on the raw data, and the Git pane undoes it; Claude Code's /rewind cannot, because R code made the change. Instructions and skills are requests that the model may or may not follow."} ::::: {.dia-flow} ::: {.dia-label} Route 1: the agent's edit tool ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-ai} Agent asks to edit `data/raw/scratch.csv` ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} edit tool ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-blocked} Deny rule refuses ::: ::::: ::::: {.dia-flow} ::: {.dia-label} Route 2: R code the agent runs ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-ai} Agent runs `writeLines()` on the same file ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} approval prompt only ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-file} File changed ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} detected by ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-check} `git status` (and, from Block 7, a checksum test on the raw data) ::: ::: {.dia-arrow} undone by ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-check} The Git pane's **Revert**. Not `/rewind`: it tracks only the edit tool's changes ::: ::::: ::::: {.dia-flow} ::: {.dia-label} Requests, on every route ::: ::: {.dia-node .dia-plain} `AGENTS.md` and skills: the model may or may not follow them ::: ::::: ::: {.dia-caption} With no hook registered, only the approval prompt stands between R code and the file, and only git can undo what it writes. Prevent where you can, detect everywhere, and commit first. And test every control: one you have not seen refuse something is one you are assuming. ::: :::::: ::::::: :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ## How it works: where the rules live Your repository's `.claude/settings.json` starts the project in **Manual** mode (`"defaultMode": "default"`: it asks before every edit and command). It also holds 17 deny rules. They protect the raw data, the data provider's note, the codebook, the checks, the references, the lockfileThe renv.lock file that records the R version and the exact package versions a project uses, so renv::restore() can rebuild the same environment. and the settings themselves. You never need to edit the file: `/permissions` shows the rules and adds new ones. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` json { "permissions": { "defaultMode": "default", "deny": [ "Edit(/data/raw/**)", "Read(/docs/data_note.md)", "Edit(/docs/data_note.md)", "Edit(/docs/codebook.csv)", "Edit(/scripts/02_validate.R)", "Edit(/scripts/03_audit_cleaning.R)", "Edit(/scripts/functions/validate_voles.R)", "Edit(/tests/fixtures/**)", "Edit(/tests/make_reference.R)", "Edit(/tests/test_cleaning.R)", "Edit(/renv.lock)", "Edit(/.github/**)", "Edit(/.claude/**)", "Edit(/.posit/**)", "Edit(/hooks/**)", "Read(/.Renviron)", "Read(/.env)" ] } } ``` ::: ::: A leading `/` anchors a pattern to the project root. `Read` and `Edit` rules cover Claude Code's own file tools, simple file commands it recognises (such as `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed` and `tee`) and shell redirects (`> file`). They do not cover R code that it runs, or a command that never names the file, such as a search of the whole project with `grep -r`. The documentation does not list `rm`, `mv` or `cp`. The rules protect named files rather than whole folders, so the agent can still write its scripts and tests in Blocks 7 and 8. `Edit(/renv.lock)` keeps `renv::status()` a real check. **Why the shared settings file.** `/permissions` can save a rule to `.claude/settings.json`, which is committed with the project, or to the local `.claude/settings.local.json`, which git ignores. Only a rule in the shared file reaches a commit, and so reaches everyone who clones the repository. Answering *don't ask again* saves an allow rule, usually in the local file. That is why `test_controls.R` checks that no command is approved in advance. ::: :::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Using another tool The exercises use Claude Code. **Posit Assistant** sets permissions per tool in `.posit/assistant/settings.json` (for example `"bash": {"rm *": "deny"}`). `deny` rules hold in every mode, including auto and YOLO. It has no documented path rules for file edits, so rely on the Git pane in step 4 of Exercise 2. It blocks reading `.env` and `.Renviron` by default. ::: :::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Instructor: demonstration of a guard hook A hookA command the assistant runs automatically at a fixed point, for example before every tool call. A hook can block the call, but it matches text, so a differently written command can get past it. is a command that Claude Code itself (the harnessThe software around a model that keeps the conversation, sends it to the model, runs the tools the model asks for and sends back their results. Claude Code is a harness; so is a chat object made with ellmer., not the model) runs before every tool callA single action an agent takes, such as reading a file, editing a file or running a shell command. Permission rules and hooks act on tool calls.. So it does not depend on the model following a request. Your instructor saves the guard hook from *Going further* as `hooks/guard_protected_paths.R` (the template does not ship `hooks/`). They register it, run *Test the hook before you trust it* on the demonstration machine, and repeat step 4. The hook, written in R, blocks any call that mentions `data/raw`, so it blocks this one before any approval prompt. Then they try the same write using `here::here("data", "raw", "scratch.csv")`. The text `data/raw` never appears, so the hook lets it through. A text-matching hook is a tripwire, not a wall; the Git pane still shows the change. The GitHub review gate (CODEOWNERSA GitHub file listing who must review changes to which paths. With branch protection, a pull request that touches those paths cannot merge without their review., branch protectionGitHub repository settings that stop changes reaching a branch such as main unless conditions are met, for example a passing check and an approved review.) is set up in the self-study page on [GitHub Copilot's cloud agent](11l-copilot-cloud-agent.qmd). ::: :::{.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Do you need a hook? The workshop ships no hooks. Before you add one to your own project, ask these questions in order: 1. **Can a deny rule say it?** If the danger is a named file or a named command, use a rule: it needs no code and nothing to maintain. 2. **Must it hold whatever route the agent takes?** Then neither a rule nor a hook is enough. Keep the thing out of reach (outside the project, or behind the sandbox where it is available), and detect changes with git or a checksum. 3. **Is it "every time X happens, do Y"?** For example: run `lintr` or `styler` after each edit, run the tests before the agent says it is finished, notify you when it is waiting, or log every call. That is what hooks are for. 4. **Is it a judgement call?** For example, "prefer a mixed model when animals are measured twice". Then write an instruction or a skill ([Block 4](11e-instructions-skills.qmd)). A hook has costs: - **It is code.** It needs testing (*Test the hook before you trust it*, in *Going further*) and keeping up to date. - **It runs on every matching call.** A hook written in R adds R's start-up time to each one. - **It fails open by default.** If it crashes, the call goes ahead. From Claude Code v2.1.295, adding `"onFailure": "block"` to the hook makes a crash block the call instead. - **It must match every route.** On Windows, Claude Code often runs commands through its PowerShell tool, so a hook that checks commands must match `PowerShell` as well as `Bash`. - **It never approves anything.** A hook can only add a check: a call it lets through still faces your usual approval prompt. **Ways to set one up:** - Add a `hooks` block to `.claude/settings.json` yourself, as in *A guard hook*, in *Going further*. - Ask Claude to draft the script and the settings for you, then read them and paste them in yourself. In the workshop repository, the deny rules keep it out of `.claude/` and `hooks/`. - Set the environment variable `CLAUDE_CODE_NEW_INIT=1` before you run `/init`. Claude Code then asks which of instruction files, skills and hooks to set up, explores the project, and shows you a proposal before it writes anything. Two cautions: - if you let it set up instruction files, it writes a `CLAUDE.md`, which hides an existing `AGENTS.md` ([Block 4](11e-instructions-skills.qmd)); - once `Edit(/.claude/**)` is in place, its writes to the settings are refused, so run it before you add that rule. To see which hooks are registered, type `/hooks`. ::: :::{.callout-note} ## Check · Reproduce · Record - **You can now:** let an agent work in Manual mode in a repository where raw data, references and checks are protected, **trusted because** you have seen a deny rule refuse, seen git catch and undo the route it misses, and have a test that fails if the rules are weakened. - **Check:** watch every control refuse something, and find the route it does not cover. What gets past the rules shows in the Git pane, Block 7's checksumA short fingerprint computed from a file’s contents, for example with tools::md5sum(). Any change to the file changes the checksum, so it detects changes made by any route. test or `test_controls.R`. - **Reproduce:** the rules live in `.claude/settings.json`, committed with the project, so everyone who clones it gets the same protection. Commit before each agent task: git can undo any change since then, and `/rewind` cannot undo what R code wrote. - **Record:** your log line from step 6 notes which requests were refused and what git caught. ::: ## Set up guardrails in your own project Your workshop repository came with its guardrails. A new project of your own starts with none, so set them up before the agent's first task. This is not covered live; it takes about 15 minutes. 1. **Version tracking first.** In the R console, run `usethis::use_git()`, then make a first commit. From then on, commit before every agent task. To undo, use `/rewind` for changes Claude made with its edit tools, and the Git pane for everything else. 2. **Permissions.** Download the starter `settings.json` below and save it as `.claude/settings.json`. Edit the paths to match your project. It starts in Manual mode and protects raw data, test references, the lockfile, credentials and itself. Add project-specific rules with `/permissions`. 3. **Instructions.** Copy the *Version control* section of your workshop `AGENTS.md` into your project's instruction file. 4. **Hooks, only if you need one.** Work through *Do you need a hook?*, above. If you will let `/init` set hooks up, run it before step 2, because `Edit(/.claude/**)` refuses its writes to the settings. 5. **Test it.** Ask the agent to edit a protected file, and watch the rule refuse. Copy `tests/test_controls.R` and change its list of rules to yours. Delete the tests for the `AGENTS.md` canary and `test_summary_functions.R`, unless your project has them. Then commit. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: :::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Reference: the starter `settings.json` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` json { "permissions": { "defaultMode": "default", "deny": [ "Edit(/data/raw/**)", "Edit(/tests/fixtures/**)", "Edit(/renv.lock)", "Edit(/.claude/**)", "Read(/.Renviron)", "Read(/.env)" ] } } ``` ::: ::: ::: **Let Claude draft rules, never decide them.** You can ask it to propose deny rules for a project, but read each one. A rule with a wrong path, such as a missing leading `/`, protects nothing and fails silently. Claude Code asks before every write to `.claude/`. The starter file's `Edit(/.claude/**)` refuses such writes outright, so you install the rules yourself. Protecting something new takes 30 seconds in `/permissions`. For confidential data, add the five habits in [Block 3](11d-context-disclosure-autonomy.qmd). Settings and hooks are code, so trust only repositories whose configuration you have read. ## Check your understanding **Which control detects a change to raw data made by any route?**
**In Exercise 2, why could the R code change `data/raw/scratch.csv` when the deny rule refused the direct edit?**
## Going further (not covered live) This material is not covered in the live session. Work through it afterwards if it is useful to you. :::::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## A guard hook Claude Code itself, the harness rather than the model, runs a `PreToolUse` hook before each tool call. It passes the hook the pending call as JSON on standard input (stdin). If the hook exits with status 2, the call is denied and its message is passed to the model. Exit status 0 does not approve the call: it goes on to your usual approval prompt. Claude Code and Posit Assistant use the same shape for this, so one script can serve both. The guard below is written in R. It denies any edit, shell command or R code that mentions a protected path. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} #!/usr/bin/env Rscript # hooks/guard_protected_paths.R ---- # PreToolUse guard for Claude Code and Posit Assistant. # Reads the pending tool call from stdin and exits 2 (deny) if the call # mentions a protected path. A tripwire, not a wall: see "Break your own # guard". protected <- c( "data/raw", "tests/fixtures", "make_reference.R", ".github/workflows" ) payload <- jsonlite::fromJSON( paste(readLines(file("stdin"), warn = FALSE), collapse = "\n"), simplifyVector = FALSE ) # search the whole tool input as text, so the same rule covers file edits, # shell commands and R code whatever the tool calls its fields call_text <- as.character(jsonlite::toJSON(payload$tool_input, auto_unbox = TRUE)) hits <- protected[vapply(protected, \(p) grepl(p, call_text, fixed = TRUE), logical(1))] if (length(hits) > 0) { message( "Blocked by project guard: this ", payload$tool_name, " call refers to a protected path (", paste(hits, collapse = ", "), "). ", "Do not modify protected files; ask the user to do it." ) quit(save = "no", status = 2) } quit(save = "no", status = 0) ``` ::: The template does not ship `hooks/`: save the script yourself as `hooks/guard_protected_paths.R`, for example with `usethis::edit_file("hooks/guard_protected_paths.R")`. It runs with `Rscript --vanilla`, so it does not start renv. `jsonlite` must be installed in your user library. **Register it with Claude Code** by adding a `hooks` key to `.claude/settings.json`, alongside the existing `permissions` key. The deny rules protect `.claude/`, so make this edit yourself, not through the agent. ```json { "hooks": { "PreToolUse": [ { "matcher": "Edit|Write|Bash|PowerShell", "hooks": [ { "type": "command", "command": "Rscript --vanilla \"$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR\"/hooks/guard_protected_paths.R", "onFailure": "block" } ] } ] } } ``` The `matcher` lists the tool names the hook runs for. On Windows, Claude Code often runs commands with its PowerShell tool rather than `Bash`, so a guard that matches only `Bash` would never see them. `"onFailure": "block"` makes the call fail if the hook itself crashes (Claude Code v2.1.295 or later; on older versions, delete that line and rely on the test below). Type `/hooks` to check that Claude Code has registered it. **Register it with Posit Assistant** in `.posit/assistant/settings.json`. The tool names differ: `edit`, `bash`, and `executeR` for R code run in your session. ```json { "hooks": { "PreToolUse": [ { "matcher": "edit|bash|executeR", "hooks": [ { "type": "command", "command": "Rscript --vanilla hooks/guard_protected_paths.R" } ] } ] } } ``` Posit Assistant runs project hooks only in a workspace you have trusted. :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Test the hook before you trust it :::: ::::{.task-container} **Goal:** check that the guard denies a protected path and allows a harmless call, so that you know it works before you rely on it. Hooks fail open by default. If the script crashes, for example because `jsonlite` is not installed, both tools continue as if the hook had allowed the call, unless you set `"onFailure": "block"` in Claude Code. Even then, a hook that runs but checks the wrong thing allows everything. So test the script directly, without the agent. The R below runs the hook exactly as Claude Code does: as a fresh `Rscript --vanilla` process, given the tool call on standard input. It works the same on Windows, macOS and Linux. **In the R console:** ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} rscript <- file.path(R.home("bin"), "Rscript") hook <- shQuote(here::here("hooks", "guard_protected_paths.R")) run_hook <- function(json) { status <- system2(rscript, c("--vanilla", hook), input = json, stdout = FALSE, stderr = FALSE) status } # can the hook's own R session load jsonlite? 0 means yes print(system2(rscript, c("--vanilla", "-e", shQuote("library(jsonlite)")), stdout = FALSE, stderr = FALSE)) # a call naming a protected path: expect 2 run_hook('{"tool_name":"Bash","tool_input":{"command":"Rscript tests/make_reference.R"}}') # a harmless call: expect 0 run_hook('{"tool_name":"Bash","tool_input":{"command":"Rscript scripts/05_analysis.R"}}') ``` ::: Any result other than 2 for the first call and 0 for the second means the hook is broken and is silently allowing everything. Now repeat the request from step 4 of Exercise 2. The R code mentions `data/raw`, so the guard should deny it before you see an approval prompt. To see exactly what each tool sends to hooks, add a temporary `PostToolUse` hook with no matcher. Make it append its input to a log file, then read the log. This is the general limit of hooks that match text: they catch the obvious form of a dangerous action, not every way of expressing it. There, the controls are on the repository itself: CODEOWNERS, branch protection and a CI check. The self-study page [Self-study: Hand a task to GitHub Copilot's cloud agent](11l-copilot-cloud-agent.qmd) sets them up. ::: :::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Feedback hooks: useful, with a warning Hooks can do more than block. A `PostToolUse` hook can run `lintr` on each R file the agent edits and pass the result back to it. A `Stop` hook can run the test suite and refuse to let the agent finish while tests fail. The second is powerful and dangerous: an agent that is told it cannot stop until tests pass may try to change the tests. Use it only when the deny rules and guard hook protect `tests/`. ::: ## Glossary ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
term definition
branch protection GitHub repository settings that stop changes reaching a branch such as main unless conditions are met, for example a passing check and an approved review.
checksum A short fingerprint computed from a file's contents, for example with tools::md5sum(). Any change to the file changes the checksum, so it detects changes made by any route.
CODEOWNERS A GitHub file listing who must review changes to which paths. With branch protection, a pull request that touches those paths cannot merge without their review.
deny rule A permission rule in the deny list of .claude/settings.json that stops Claude Code's built-in tools from editing or reading the matching files. It checks shell output redirects such as > file, but not R code or most other commands that change the same files.
harness The software around a model that keeps the conversation, sends it to the model, runs the tools the model asks for and sends back their results. Claude Code is a harness; so is a chat object made with ellmer.
hook A command the assistant runs automatically at a fixed point, for example before every tool call. A hook can block the call, but it matches text, so a differently written command can get past it.
instruction file A file the assistant loads into every conversation, such as AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md, stating the project's standing conventions. Its contents are requests, not guarantees.
lockfile The renv.lock file that records the R version and the exact package versions a project uses, so renv::restore() can rebuild the same environment.
tool call A single action an agent takes, such as reading a file, editing a file or running a shell command. Permission rules and hooks act on tool calls.
